question:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
A.Shalini was scrolling down the phone screen while waiting for her friend.
B.Her friend brought a bouquet for Shalini from the market place.
C.When her friend arrived, they went to the market place.
D.The market place was thronging with people.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. ACDB.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Sentence A is the best opening line as it introduces Shalini and sets the scene — she is waiting for her friend and scrolling through her phone. It has no pronoun referring back to anything, so it must start the paragraph.

• Sentence C logically follows A: it tells us "when her friend arrived", directly continuing from A where Shalini was waiting for the friend to arrive; they then went to the market place together.

• Sentence D follows C by describing the market place they had just reached — "was thronging with people" — giving a description of the scene at the market.

• Sentence B logically comes last, as the concluding action: "Her friend brought a bouquet for Shalini from the market place", which is the outcome/result of the visit to the market described in C and D.

Therefore, the correct order is A-C-D-B, and the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (BACD) is incorrect because it starts with B, the concluding action (the friend giving the bouquet), before the market visit has even been introduced — this reverses cause and effect.

• Option 2 (DACB) is incorrect because it opens with D, a description of the crowded market place, before the reader even knows that anyone has gone to the market — this sentence has no context without C preceding it.

• Option 3 (ABCD) is incorrect because it places B (friend brought a bouquet from the market) before C (they went to the market place) — the bouquet could not have been brought from the market before the visit to the market is even mentioned.

NOTE

• In parajumble questions, always look for the independent/topic sentence first — a sentence that introduces the subject without depending on a pronoun or connector from another sentence.

• Watch for linking words and time markers ("when", "then", "thus", "therefore") — they usually indicate which sentence follows which.

• Sentences describing a result or consequence almost always come at the end of the paragraph, as seen with sentence B here.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Cut a poor figure
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. To put a bad impression.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Cut a poor figure" means to make a bad or unimpressive impression on others, especially through one's appearance, performance or behaviour. (बुरा प्रभाव डालना)
◦ Example: He cut a poor figure at the interview because he was underprepared and nervous.

• The word "figure" here refers to the impression or image a person presents to others, and "poor" qualifies it as weak or unimpressive.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "In a poor state" describes a condition of poverty or a bad situation, not the act of creating an impression — this is not the meaning of the idiom.

• Option 2: "To put a good impression" is the exact opposite of the idiom's actual meaning — this idiom is negative, not positive.

• Option 4: "Bad physical form" wrongly takes "figure" literally as a person's body shape, whereas in this idiom "figure" refers to one's overall impression, not physical fitness.

NOTE

• The opposite idiom, "Cut a fine/good figure", means to make a good impression.

• Other idioms with "figure": "a figure of speech" (an expressive, non-literal use of language) and "to figure out" (to understand or solve something).

• Common SSC idioms of impression: "to make a mark" (to become notable) and "to leave much to be desired" (to be unsatisfactory).

question:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in correct order.
A 2007–2009 study
P. explored forward thinking techniques
Q. to synchronise time on board deep
R. space probes for accurate navigation, in
S. particular looking into low-cost options
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. PQRS.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The fixed opening phrase "A 2007–2009 study" needs a verb to complete its subject — P ("explored forward thinking techniques") supplies this verb naturally, so P must come first.

• P must be followed by Q ("to synchronise time on board deep"), since "explored forward thinking techniques" needs a purpose/infinitive clause — "techniques to synchronise time" makes logical sense.

• Q ends mid-phrase with "deep", which grammatically continues into R ("space probes for accurate navigation, in") — forming "deep space probes for accurate navigation".

• R ends with "in", which is completed by S ("particular looking into low-cost options") — forming the fixed phrase "in particular".

• Reading the full sentence: "A 2007–2009 study explored forward thinking techniques to synchronise time on board deep space probes for accurate navigation, in particular looking into low-cost options." This is grammatically complete and coherent.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (RSPQ) is incorrect because it begins with R ("space probes for accurate navigation, in"), which cannot directly follow "A 2007–2009 study" without a verb.

• Option 2 (PSRQ) is incorrect because after P ("explored forward thinking techniques"), S ("particular looking into low-cost options") creates a meaningless jump — "techniques particular looking into" is ungrammatical.

• Option 3 (SPRQ) is incorrect because it starts with S ("particular looking into low-cost options"), which cannot logically follow "A 2007–2009 study" as an opening clause.

NOTE

• In such sentence-part rearrangement questions, first identify split phrases across two parts (like "deep" + "space probes", and "in" + "particular") — they must always stay adjacent.

• Look for the part that contains the main verb to decide what follows the fixed opening phrase.

• Read the final reconstructed sentence aloud (mentally) to confirm it makes complete grammatical and logical sense.

question:
Select the correct passive form of the given sentence.
The indentured labourers fix the roads.
option_1: The roads was fixed by indentured labourers.
option_2: The roads were fixed by indentured labourers.
option_3: The roads are fixed by indentured labourers.
option_4: The roads were being fixed by indentured labourers.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The roads are fixed by indentured labourers.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "The indentured labourers fix the roads" is in the Simple Present Tense.

• Rule — Simple Present Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + V1/V5 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + is/am/are + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "the roads" becomes the subject of the passive sentence; since "roads" is plural, the auxiliary verb must be "are"; the verb "fix" becomes the past participle "fixed"; and "the indentured labourers" becomes the agent introduced by "by".
◦ Passive: The roads are fixed by indentured labourers.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "was" is a singular past-tense auxiliary, but the subject "roads" is plural and the tense must remain present, not past.

• Option 2 is incorrect because "were fixed" is the passive form of the Simple Past Tense ("fixed"), not the Simple Present Tense used in the given active sentence.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "were being fixed" is the passive form of the Past Continuous Tense, which does not match the Simple Present Tense of the original sentence.

NOTE

• Always match the tense of the passive auxiliary to the tense of the active sentence — do not shift tense while converting voice.

• Always check subject-verb (number) agreement in the passive object-turned-subject: singular subject takes "is", plural subject takes "are".

• Only transitive verbs (verbs that take a direct object) can be changed into the passive voice.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice.
The evil king was defeated by Gandolf, the savior.
option_1: Gandolf, the savior, defeated the evil king.
option_2: The savior of Gandolf defeated the evil king.
option_3: Gandolf, the savior, had defeated the evil king.
option_4: Gandolf, the savior, defeats the evil king.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Gandolf, the savior, defeated the evil king.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "The evil king was defeated by Gandolf, the savior" is in the Simple Past Tense, Passive Voice (was + V3).

• Rule — Simple Past Tense:
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + V3 + by + Subject
◦ Active: Subject + V2 + Object

• Applying the rule: the agent "Gandolf, the savior" (after "by") becomes the subject; the past participle "defeated" becomes the simple past verb "defeated" (V2, same form here); and "the evil king" becomes the object.
◦ Active: Gandolf, the savior, defeated the evil king.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect because it wrongly rewrites "Gandolf, the savior" as "The savior of Gandolf", which changes the meaning by making "savior" a separate person possessing Gandolf, rather than an appositive identifying Gandolf himself.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "had defeated" is the Past Perfect Tense, which is not the tense of the original passive sentence ("was defeated" is Simple Past).

• Option 4 is incorrect because "defeats" is Simple Present Tense, whereas the original sentence is in the Simple Past Tense.

NOTE

• The phrase set off by commas ("the savior") is an appositive — it renames or describes the noun before it ("Gandolf") and must stay attached to it during voice conversion, never rearranged into a possessive.

• Always keep the tense identical between active and passive forms; only the structure (subject-object order and auxiliary) changes, not the tense.

• The by-agent in a passive sentence always becomes the subject in the active sentence.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Bear the palm
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. To be a winner.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Bear the palm" means to win, to be victorious, or to be regarded as the best/first in a competition. (विजयी होना)
◦ Example: After years of hard work, she finally bore the palm in the state-level chess championship.

• The idiom originates from the ancient practice of awarding a palm branch or palm leaf to the winner of a contest as a symbol of victory and honour.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "To bring joyful news" is unrelated to victory; a closer idiom for this meaning would be "to bring glad tidings".

• Option 2: "To lose a game" is the exact opposite of the idiom's meaning — "bear the palm" signifies winning, not losing.

• Option 3: "To advocate peace" confuses "palm" with the unrelated symbol of the "olive branch", which represents peace, not this idiom.

NOTE

• Do not confuse the palm branch (victory) with the olive branch (peace) — both are plant-based symbols but represent different ideas.

• Other idioms of victory/success often asked in SSC: "to carry the day" (to win), "to win hands down" (to win easily), and "to steal the show" (to attract the most attention/praise).

question:
A sentence has been given with a blank to be filled with an appropriate word. Choose the correct alternative.
Every person should know their own _______, what their skill set is and how unique they are.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. specialties.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence explains that a person should know their own "specialties" — that is, their particular skills, strengths, or areas of expertise — which fits perfectly with the following clause, "what their skill set is and how unique they are".

• "Specialties" means the special skills, subjects, or qualities in which a person excels; the sentence is directly explaining this term through the phrase "skill set" and "unique", confirming that it is the correct fit.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "calamities" means disasters or serious misfortunes, which has no logical connection with "skill set" or being "unique".

• Option 2: "punctualities" is not a standard usable word in this sense (punctuality is normally uncountable) and refers to being on time, unrelated to skills.

• Option 4: "fecundities" relates to fertility or the capacity to produce offspring/abundant results, which is completely unrelated to the context of skills or uniqueness.

NOTE

• In fill-in-the-blank vocabulary questions, always check the surrounding clause for a definition or explanation clue — here, "what their skill set is and how unique they are" directly defines the missing word.

• Commonly confused word pairs in SSC vocabulary questions: specialty vs. speciality (both acceptable, American vs. British usage), and skill vs. specialty vs. expertise.

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
The manager told her that / she should be a bit more / careful while executed the / orders of the company.
option_2: she should be a bit more
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. careful while executed the.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule: After the conjunction "while", when the subject of the subordinate clause is the same as the subject of the main clause, the verb must take the gerund (V1 + ing) form, not the past tense/past participle form.

• In the given sentence, the segment reads "careful while executed the", where "executed" is wrongly used instead of the gerund "executing".

• The correct segment should read: "careful while executing the".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 ("The manager told her that") is grammatically correct — "told" correctly introduces reported speech with the conjunction "that".

• Option 2 ("she should be a bit more") is grammatically correct — "should be" is a correct modal + "be" construction, and "a bit more" correctly modifies the adjective that follows.

• Option 3 ("orders of the company") is grammatically correct — it is a properly formed noun phrase completing the sentence.

NOTE

• Conjunctions like "while", "before", "after", "since" are commonly followed by a gerund (V-ing) when no new subject is introduced.

• Compare: "He hurt himself while playing football" (correct) vs. "He hurt himself while played football" (incorrect).

• This is a frequently tested SSC error-spotting pattern — always check verb forms following subordinating conjunctions.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
A loud appeal or demand
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Clamour.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Clamour" means a loud and vehement appeal, demand, or outcry, especially from a group of people. (शोर-शराबा करके मांग करना)
◦ Example: There was a public clamour for the resignation of the corrupt minister.

• The word captures both the ideas of loudness and demand/appeal, exactly matching the given definition.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Protest" (विरोध) means a strong objection or expression of disapproval — it need not be "loud" and is about opposing something, not appealing/demanding something.

• Option 2: "Entourage" (अनुचर वर्ग) means a group of people who attend or surround an important person, which is unrelated to a loud appeal.

• Option 4: "Gambit" (चाल) means an opening move or action, especially in chess or a negotiation, intended to gain an advantage — unrelated to loudness or demand.

NOTE

• Related words: "outcry" (a loud protest or clamour) and "uproar" (a loud noise or commotion, often of protest).

• Do not confuse "clamour" (loud demand) with "calumny" (a false and malicious statement, i.e., slander) — the two are commonly confused because of similar spelling.

question: Select the sentences that contains no spelling errors.
option_1: He screeched hystericalli after seeing the accident.
option_2: He screeched hystericaly after seeing the accident.
option_3: He screeched hysteerically after seeing the accident.
option_4: He screeched hysterically after seeing the accident.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. He screeched hysterically after seeing the accident.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "hysterically" — the adverb formed from the adjective "hysterical" (meaning in an uncontrolled, extremely emotional manner) by adding "-ly".

• Spelling key: HYSTER + IC + AL + LY. Note the sequence "ic-al" before the adverbial "-ly" ending, and only a single "s" and single "r".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "hystericalli" is incorrect — the ending has been wrongly written as "-calli" instead of "-cally".

• Option 2: "hystericaly" is incorrect — it is missing the "c" and has only a single "l" where the correct ending needs "-ically".

• Option 3: "hysteerically" is incorrect — it has an extra "e" inserted after "hyst", making it "hysteer-" instead of "hyster-".

NOTE

• Adverbs formed from adjectives ending in "-ic" or "-ical" almost always end in "-ically" (e.g., basically, dramatically, historically, systematically) — not "-icly" or "-icalli".

• Practise similar frequently misspelt SSC words: "specifically", "automatically", "tragically".

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.
He said, ‘Let us wait for the award.’
option_1: He proposed that they should wait for the award.
option_2: He said that he should wait for the award.
option_3: He proposed that he should wait for the award.
option_4: He said that they should waited for the award.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. He proposed that they should wait for the award.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule: When direct speech begins with "Let us" (making a proposal or suggestion), the reporting verb "said" is changed to "proposed" / "suggested", the word "that" is added, and "Let us" is replaced with "they/we + should", followed by the base verb.

• Since the sentence does not indicate that the speaker is including only himself and the listener exclusively, the standard SSC convention converts "us" to "they", giving "that they should wait".

• Applying the rule: He said, "Let us wait for the award." → He proposed that they should wait for the award.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect because it retains the reporting verb "said" instead of changing it to "proposed/suggested", and it wrongly uses "he" instead of "they" for "us".

• Option 3 is incorrect because although it correctly changes the verb to "proposed", it wrongly converts "us" to "he" instead of "they".

• Option 4 is incorrect because it retains "said" instead of "proposed/suggested", and it wrongly uses the past tense "waited" instead of the correct modal construction "should wait".

NOTE

• The "Let us" rule is a frequently tested exception in narration: it does NOT follow the normal tense-backshift rule of the reported verb.

• Other "Let" patterns: "Let him/her/them + V1" is reported as "said that + subject + should/might + V1", keeping the reporting verb "said".

• "Let us" expressing a proposal must be distinguished from "Let" used for permission (e.g., "Let me go" → "He requested that he be allowed to go").

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Humble
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Arrogant.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Humble" means having or showing a modest or low estimate of one's own importance. (विनम्र)

• "Arrogant" means having an exaggerated sense of one's own importance or abilities, often displayed in an overbearing manner. (अहंकारी) — this is the direct opposite of being humble.
◦ Example: He remained humble despite his success, unlike his arrogant colleague who boasted constantly.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Dishonour" (अपमान) means a state of shame or disgrace — it is a noun about loss of respect, not an adjective opposite of "humble".

• Option 2: "Pleasantry" (शिष्टाचारपूर्ण बातचीत) means a polite or friendly remark, which is unrelated in meaning to "humble".

• Option 3: "Modest" (विनम्र) is actually a synonym of "humble", not its antonym — both describe a lack of excessive pride.

NOTE

• Common confusion in antonym questions: options that are synonyms of the given word (like "Modest" here) are deliberately placed as distractors — always double-check whether an option means the same or the opposite.

• Other antonym pairs of "humble": humble ↔ proud, humble ↔ haughty, humble ↔ conceited.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
During my Goa tour, I had visited beaches in Vasco, Baga and Vagator.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. visited.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence describes a single, completed past action — visiting beaches during a specific past event, "my Goa tour" — with no earlier past action being referred to for comparison.

• Rule — Simple Past Tense is used for an action that started and finished at a definite time in the past, especially when a time-bound phrase like "During my Goa tour" is present.
◦ Structure: Subject + V2 (past form)

• "Had visited" (past perfect) is incorrect here because the past perfect tense is used only to show an action that happened before another past action, and no such second past action is mentioned in the sentence.

• The correct sentence: "During my Goa tour, I visited beaches in Vasco, Baga and Vagator."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "have visited" is the Present Perfect Tense, which is used for actions connected to the present, not for a definite past event like "during my Goa tour".

• Option 3: "was visited" wrongly uses the passive voice; the subject "I" is the doer of the action, so a passive construction is grammatically inappropriate here.

• Option 4: "had visited" (the original underlined phrase) is incorrect for the reason explained above — there is no earlier past action for it to precede.

NOTE

• The Past Perfect Tense ("had + V3") is used only when two past actions are being compared, to show which one happened first.

• A time expression like "during", "in [year]", "last week" etc., without any second past event, is a strong signal that the Simple Past Tense is required, not the Past Perfect.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The country’s rapid _________ has led to a rise in many people’s standard of living.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. growth.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence talks about a rise in "standard of living", which is a direct consequence of a country's economic and developmental "growth" — a rapid increase in production, income, and infrastructure.

• "Growth" collocates naturally with "rapid" ("rapid growth") and logically causes an improved standard of living, making it the only word that completes the sentence's cause-effect relationship correctly.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "idea" does not logically fit — a country's "rapid idea" is meaningless and has no cause-effect link with a rise in standard of living.

• Option 2: "life" does not collocate with "rapid" in this context and does not describe a measurable cause of a rise in living standards.

• Option 3: "confidence" could describe a psychological state but a country's rapid "confidence" is not standard usage, and it is not the typical driver of a rise in standard of living — economic growth is.

NOTE

• Common SSC collocations with "rapid": rapid growth, rapid development, rapid expansion, rapid progress, rapid increase.

• "Standard of living" is most commonly linked in exam passages with words like economy, growth, development, income, and GDP.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the word laborious from the given sentence:
Although gardening is a laborious job, but it gives me boundless joy, strenuous happiness and immense satisfaction and I like this facile activity.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. facile.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Laborious" means requiring considerable time, effort, and hard work; difficult and tiring. (श्रमसाध्य)

• "Facile" means easily achieved or done, requiring little effort. (सरल/आसान) — this is the direct opposite of "laborious".
◦ Example: Unlike the laborious first attempt, the second solution was quite facile.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "boundless" (असीम) means having no limits, describing the joy in the sentence — it does not mean the opposite of "difficult/hard work".

• Option 3: "strenuous" (कठिन/परिश्रमी) means requiring great physical or mental effort — this is actually close in meaning to "laborious", not its opposite.

• Option 4: "immense" (विशाल/अत्यधिक) means extremely large in size or degree, describing the satisfaction mentioned — it is unrelated to the ease/difficulty of work.

NOTE

• Be careful in "antonym from the sentence" questions — words that seem similar in tone (like "strenuous", which resembles "laborious" in meaning) are common distractors.

• Other synonyms of "facile": effortless, easy, simple, straightforward — and other synonyms of "laborious": arduous, toilsome, onerous, gruelling.

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Friwsk.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Friwsk" is not a correctly spelt English word. The intended word appears to be "Frisk", meaning to search a person by feeling their clothes/body for hidden items, or to move around playfully and energetically.

• Spelling key for the correct word: F + R + I + S + K — there is no "w" in the word "frisk".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Reply" (उत्तर) is correctly spelt — meaning an answer given to a question or statement.

• Option 3: "Rusk" (सूखा हुआ मीठा बिस्किट) is correctly spelt — meaning a hard, dry biscuit or piece of bread.

• Option 4: "Foliage" (पत्ते/पत्ते-समूह) is correctly spelt — meaning the leaves of a plant collectively.

NOTE

• In "identify the incorrectly spelt word" questions, check each option letter by letter — an extra, missing, or swapped letter (like the extra "w" here) is the most common type of error.

• Practise other commonly tested spelling words: friction, frisky, rustic, foliage, foliation.

question:
Select the most appropriate adverb to fill in the blank.
They supplied the required human resource ____________.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. faultlessly.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires an adverb to modify the verb "supplied", describing HOW the human resource was supplied.

• "Faultlessly" means without any error or mistake; perfectly — it is formed by adding the adverbial suffix "-ly" to the adjective "faultless", and it correctly modifies the verb "supplied".

• Rule: Adverbs of manner typically end in "-ly" and answer the question "how?" about a verb — only "faultlessly" among the given options is grammatically an adverb.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "heavy" is an adjective, not an adverb (the adverb form would be "heavily"), so it cannot grammatically modify the verb "supplied" in this slot.

• Option 3: "clear" is primarily an adjective (the adverb form would be "clearly"); using "clear" here would be grammatically incorrect as an adverb of manner.

• Option 4: "able" is an adjective describing capability (used with "to" as in "able to"), not an adverb, and cannot fit grammatically in this blank.

NOTE

• Most adverbs of manner are formed by adding "-ly" to an adjective: faultless → faultlessly, careful → carefully, quick → quickly.

• Always check the part of speech required by the blank — here, since a verb ("supplied") is being modified, an adverb (not an adjective) is required.

• Common irregular adverbs to remember: good → well, fast → fast, hard → hard (same form as adjective).

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the underlined word.
The celebrity was inundated with birthday wishes from his admirers.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Overwhelmed.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Inundated" means overwhelmed with an excessive or overpowering amount of something (originally: flooded with water). (अभिभूत/भर जाना)
◦ Example: The helpline was inundated with calls after the announcement.

• "Overwhelmed" carries the same meaning of being flooded or overpowered by a large quantity of something, making it the closest synonym.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Annoyed" (नाराज़) means irritated or bothered, which is unrelated to the idea of being flooded with something in large quantity.

• Option 2: "Preoccupied" (व्यस्त/तल्लीन) means engrossed or absorbed in thought, which does not capture the sense of being flooded with a large amount of something.

• Option 3: "Rewarded" (पुरस्कृत) means given something in recognition of effort, which is unrelated to the idea of being overwhelmed by quantity.

NOTE

• "Inundated" is literally a flood-related word (from Latin "inundare", to flood) — remember its figurative sense of being overwhelmed by a large quantity of something (mail, calls, requests, wishes).

• Similar words: deluged, flooded, swamped, overwhelmed — all mean being overloaded with something.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Dispatch
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Acquire.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Dispatch" (as a verb) means to send off to a destination or for a specific purpose. (भेजना/रवाना करना)

• "Acquire" means to obtain, gain possession of, or receive something. (प्राप्त करना) — this is the direct opposite of sending something away, as it involves receiving/obtaining instead.
◦ Example: The company will dispatch the goods today, and the buyer should acquire them by tomorrow.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Transmit" (संचारित करना) means to send or pass something from one place/person to another — this is a synonym of "dispatch", not its antonym.

• Option 3: "Deliver" (पहुँचाना) means to bring and hand over something to its destination — this is also close in meaning to "dispatch" (sending something), not its opposite.

• Option 4: "Bulletin" (विज्ञप्ति) is a noun meaning a short official statement or news update — it is not even the same part of speech as the verb "dispatch" and is unrelated in meaning.

NOTE

• Careful: several options here ("Transmit", "Deliver") are actually synonyms, not antonyms — always confirm the direction of meaning (sending vs. receiving) rather than picking any related word.

• Other antonym pairs: dispatch ↔ receive, send ↔ receive, export ↔ import.

question:
Select the correct direct form of the given sentence.
Leena said that his relatives were landing the next day.
option_2: Leena said, "His relatives are landing today."
option_3: Leena said, "His relatives were landing tomorrow."
option_4: Leena said, "His relatives are landing tomorrow."
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Leena said, "His relatives are landing tomorrow."

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule: When converting reported (indirect) speech back to direct speech, the reported past continuous tense ("were landing") is converted to the direct present continuous tense ("are landing"), since direct speech represents the exact original words spoken.

• Rule for time expressions: the reported phrase "the next day" converts back to "tomorrow" in direct speech.

• Rule for pronouns: since Leena is talking about someone else's relatives (not her own), the pronoun "his" remains "his" in the direct speech — it does not change to "my".

• Applying all three rules: Leena said that his relatives were landing the next day. → Leena said, "His relatives are landing tomorrow."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because it wrongly uses "My relatives" instead of "His relatives", and wrongly uses the simple present "land" instead of the present continuous "are landing".

• Option 2 is incorrect because it wrongly uses "today" instead of "tomorrow" — "the next day" in reported speech always converts back to "tomorrow" in direct speech, not "today".

• Option 3 is incorrect because it retains "were landing" (past continuous) in the direct speech instead of converting it back to the present continuous "are landing".

NOTE

• Direct-to-indirect (and vice versa) time-expression conversions to remember: now ↔ then, today ↔ that day, tomorrow ↔ the next day, yesterday ↔ the previous day, here ↔ there, this ↔ that.

• When converting indirect speech back to direct speech, all backshifted tenses must be reversed to their original direct-speech tense.

• Pronouns in direct speech must match the actual speaker/subject being referred to, not automatically default to first person.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Education (1)_____ both the teaching and learning of knowledge, proper conduct, and technical competency. It thus (2)____ on the cultivation of skills, trades or professions, as well as mental, moral and aesthetic development. Formal education consists of systematic instruction, teaching and training by (3)____ teachers. This consists of the application of pedagogy and the development of curricula. The right to education is a (4)_____ human right. Educational systems are established to provide education and (5)________, often for children and the young.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. encompasses.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a verb meaning "to include or comprise something as an inherent part", since the sentence explains that education "____ both the teaching and learning of knowledge, proper conduct, and technical competency" — i.e., education includes/covers all these aspects.

• "Encompasses" precisely means to include comprehensively, to cover a wide range of items or ideas, which fits the sense of education covering multiple aspects (knowledge, conduct, competency).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "likes" does not fit grammatically or logically — education cannot "like" teaching and learning; this verb expresses a preference, not inclusion.

• Option 2: "releases" means to let go or set free, which does not logically fit the idea of education containing or including these elements.

• Option 3: "makes" is too vague and does not convey the sense of comprehensive inclusion required by the sentence; "makes teaching and learning" is not idiomatic.

NOTE

• In cloze passages, always read the full sentence and surrounding context rather than the blank in isolation — here, the list of items after the blank ("teaching and learning... conduct... competency") signals a verb of inclusion is needed.

• Synonyms of "encompass": include, cover, embrace, incorporate, comprise.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Education (1)_____ both the teaching and learning of knowledge, proper conduct, and technical competency. It thus (2)____ on the cultivation of skills, trades or professions, as well as mental, moral and aesthetic development. Formal education consists of systematic instruction, teaching and training by (3)____ teachers. This consists of the application of pedagogy and the development of curricula. The right to education is a (4)_____ human right. Educational systems are established to provide education and (5)________, often for children and the young.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. focuses.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank is followed by the preposition "on" — **"It thus ____ on the cultivation of skills, trades or professions..." — and the verb "focus" is the standard collocation that pairs with "on" to mean "to concentrate attention or effort on something"**.

• The sentence logically continues from the previous one about education encompassing various aspects, now specifying that it particularly concentrates/focuses on skill-building.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "changes" does not collocate naturally with "on" in this sense and does not fit the meaning of concentrating attention on something.

• Option 2: "makes" does not collocate with "on" here ("makes on the cultivation" is not standard English) and does not convey the intended meaning.

• Option 4: "regards" typically does not take "on" as its following preposition (it usually takes "as" or no preposition, e.g., "regards it as important"), so it is grammatically inappropriate here.

NOTE

• Common collocation to remember: "focus on" (to concentrate on), as opposed to "concentrate on", "centre on", or "dwell on".

• Always check which preposition follows the blank in cloze questions — it often eliminates several distractor options immediately based on standard collocation.

question:

Education (1)_____ both the teaching and learning of knowledge, proper conduct, and technical competency. It thus (2)____ on the cultivation of skills, trades or professions, as well as mental, moral and aesthetic development. Formal education consists of systematic instruction, teaching and training by (3)____ teachers. This consists of the application of pedagogy and the development of curricula. The right to education is a (4)_____ human right. Educational systems are established to provide education and (5)________, often for children and the young.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. professional.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: **"Formal education consists of systematic instruction, teaching and training by ____ teachers." The blank must describe the kind of teachers who provide systematic, formal instruction — this calls for "professional"**, meaning trained and qualified in their field.

• "Professional teachers" is a standard, natural collocation referring to teachers who are formally trained and qualified to teach, matching the context of "formal education" and "systematic instruction".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "general" is vague and does not specifically capture the idea of trained, qualified educators delivering systematic formal instruction.

• Option 3: "fresh" refers to newness or inexperience, which is unrelated to and even somewhat contrary to the idea of qualified instruction implied by "formal education".

• Option 4: "new" similarly refers to recency, not to qualification or expertise, and does not fit the context of "systematic instruction" by trained educators.

NOTE

• "Professional" is frequently used in formal/academic passages to denote expertise and formal qualification — e.g., professional training, professional development, professional teachers.

• Do not confuse descriptive words about time/newness ("fresh", "new") with words about qualification/expertise ("professional", "qualified", "trained") in cloze passages.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Education (1)_____ both the teaching and learning of knowledge, proper conduct, and technical competency. It thus (2)____ on the cultivation of skills, trades or professions, as well as mental, moral and aesthetic development. Formal education consists of systematic instruction, teaching and training by (3)____ teachers. This consists of the application of pedagogy and the development of curricula. The right to education is a (4)_____ human right. Educational systems are established to provide education and (5)________, often for children and the young.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. fundamental.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: **"The right to education is a ____ human right." This is a well-known, fixed phrase in official and legal contexts — the "right to education" is universally described as a "fundamental human right"**, i.e., a basic, essential right guaranteed to all human beings.

• "Fundamental" means forming a necessary base or core; of central importance, which correctly conveys that education is one of the essential, foundational rights of every individual.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "personal" means relating to an individual specifically, which does not capture the universal, essential nature implied by "human right" in this context.

• Option 3: "beautiful" is an aesthetic quality and is entirely unrelated to describing the nature or importance of a legal/human right.

• Option 4: "long standing" refers to something that has existed for a long time, which does not capture the idea of being basic or essential — it describes duration, not importance.

NOTE

• "Fundamental human right" is a fixed, commonly used phrase in constitutional and international human rights contexts (e.g., UN Declaration of Human Rights) — remember it as a set collocation.

• Other similar fixed phrases: "basic human right", "inalienable right", "constitutional right".

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. training.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: **"Educational systems are established to provide education and ____, often for children and the young." The phrase "education and training"** is a common, fixed collocation used to describe the full scope of formal learning systems, covering both academic knowledge and practical/vocational skill-building.

• "Training" logically pairs with "education" as the two combined activities that educational systems are set up to deliver, especially to the young.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "dreams" does not logically pair with "education" as something an educational system is established to "provide" in this structural/institutional sense.

• Option 2: "challenges" does not fit — educational systems are not established to provide "challenges" alongside education as their stated institutional purpose.

• Option 4: "upbringing" refers to the process of raising a child, typically the responsibility of parents/family rather than of "educational systems", making it a less precise fit than "training".

NOTE

• "Education and training" is a standard fixed phrase frequently used in policy, government, and formal writing to describe combined academic and skill-based learning.

• Distinguish "upbringing" (a broader, family-based process of raising a child) from "training" (structured skill instruction, typically provided by institutions).
